L32: # The Pop-Stack Operator on Ornamentation Lattices
L33: 
L34: Khalid Ajran Address: Department of Mathematics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Email address: kajran@mit.edu and Colin Defant Address: Department of Mathematics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Email address: colindefant@gmail.com
L35: ###### Abstract.
L36: Each rooted plane tree $\mathsf{T}$ has an associated ornamentation lattice $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$. The ornamentation lattice of an $n$-element chain is the $n$-th Tamari lattice. We study the pop-stack operator $\mathsf{Pop}\colon\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})\to\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$, which sends each element $\delta$ to the meet of the elements covered by or equal to $\delta$.
L37: We compute the maximum size of a forward orbit of $\mathsf{Pop}$ on $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$, generalizing a result of Defant for Tamari lattices. We also characterize the image of $\mathsf{Pop}$ on $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$, generalizing a result of Hong for Tamari lattices. For each integer $k\geq 0$, we provide necessary conditions for an element of $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$ to be in the image of $\mathsf{Pop}^{k}$.
L38: This allows us to completely characterize the image of $\mathsf{Pop}^{k}$ on a Tamari lattice.
L39: ## 1. Introduction
L40: ### 1.1. Ornamentation Lattices
L41: Laplante-Anfossi [cite20†15 ] recently introduced remarkable polytopes called operahedra. These polytopes are special examples of graph associahedra [cite21†5 , cite22†17 ] and poset associahedra [cite23†13 ], and they generalize both the associahedra and permutohedra. Laplante-Anfossi also considered certain posets obtained by orienting the $1$-skeletons of operahedra, and he asked if these posets are lattices.
L42: Defant and Sack [cite24†11 ] answered Laplante-Anfossi’s question in the affirmative, naming his posets operahedron lattices. A key idea that Defant and Sack employed was to embed an operahedron lattice into the product of an interval in the weak order on the symmetric group and another lattice. This other lattice, which is the primary focus of this article, is a new structure called an ornamentation lattice.
L43: Let $\mathrm{PT}_{n}$ denote the set of rooted plane trees with $n$ nodes. Let $\mathsf{T}\in\mathrm{PT}_{n}$. We view $\mathsf{T}$ both as a graph and as a poset in which every non-root element is covered by exactly $1$ element (so the root is the unique maximal element). We denote the partial order on $\mathsf{T}$ by $\leq_{\mathsf{T}}$. For $v\in\mathsf{T}$, we write
L44:  | $$\Delta_{\mathsf{T}}(v)=\{v^{\prime}\in\mathsf{T}:v^{\prime}\leq_{\mathsf{T}}v\}\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla_{\mathsf{T}}(v)=\{v^{\prime}\in\mathsf{T}:v\leq_{\mathsf{T}}v^{\prime}\}.$$  |
L45: An ornament of $\mathsf{T}$ is a set of nodes that induces a connected subgraph of $\mathsf{T}$. Let $\mathrm{Orn}(\mathsf{T})$ denote the set of ornaments of $\mathsf{T}$. We will often view an ornament as a rooted plane tree. Two sets are said to be nested if one is a subset of the other. An ornamentation of $\mathsf{T}$ is a function $\delta\colon\mathsf{T}\to\mathrm{Orn}(\mathsf{T})$ such that
L46: 
L47:   * •
L48: 
L49: for every $v\in\mathsf{T}$, the unique maximal element of $\delta(v)$ is $v$;
L50: 
L51:   * •
L52: for all $v,v^{\prime}\in\mathsf{T}$, the ornaments $\delta(v)$ and $\delta(v^{\prime})$ are either nested or disjoint.
L53: 
L54: Let $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$ denote the set of ornamentations of $\mathsf{T}$. We view $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$ as a poset, where the partial order $\leq$ is defined so that $\delta\leq\delta^{\prime}$ if and only if $\delta(v)\subseteq\delta^{\prime}(v)$ for all $v\in\mathsf{T}$. Then $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$ is a lattice whose meet operation $\wedge$ is such that
L55:  | $$(\delta\wedge\delta^{\prime})(v)=\delta(v)\cap\delta^{\prime}(v)$$  |
L56: 
L57: for all $v\in\mathsf{T}$. The minimum element $\delta_{\min}$ and maximum element $\delta_{\max}$ of $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$ satisfy
L58: 
L59:  | $$\delta_{\min}(v)=\{v\}\quad\text{and}\quad\delta_{\max}(v)=\Delta_{\mathsf{T}}(v)$$  |
L60: 
L61: for all $v\in\mathsf{T}$. See cite25†Figure 1 . If $\delta\in\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$ and $v\in\mathsf{T}$, then we call $\delta(v)$ an ornament of $\delta$.
L62: Ornamentation lattices naturally generalize Tamari lattices. Indeed, the $n$-th Tamari lattice is isomorphic to the ornamentation lattice of an $n$-element chain. Tamari lattices have numerous interesting properties; we will generalize some of these properties to the much broader family of ornamentation lattices.

L65: ### 1.2. Pop-Stack Operators
L66: 
L67: The pop-stack operator of a finite lattice $L$ is the map $\mathsf{Pop}\colon L\to L$ defined by
L68: 
L69:  | $$\mathsf{Pop}(x)=\bigwedge(\{x\}\cup\{y\in L:y\lessdot x\}).$$  |
L70: Initial works on this operator focused on the case where $L$ is the weak order on the symmetric group [cite26†1 , cite27†2 , cite28†7 , cite29†8 , cite30†16 , cite31†18 , cite32†20 ], where it can be interpreted as a deterministic sorting procedure that makes use of a data structure called a pop-stack. Several recent articles have studied pop-stack operators on other interesting lattices, especially from a dynamical point of view [cite33†4 , cite34†6 , cite35†9 , cite36†10 , cite37†12 , cite38†14 ].
L71: For example, Defant [cite36†10 ] and Hong [cite38†14 ] found that the pop-stack operator on a Tamari lattice has particularly well behaved dynamics. Choi and Sun [cite34†6 ] and Barnard, Defant, and Hanson [cite33†4 ] later generalized these results to the much broader class of Cambrian lattices. In this article, we generalize the results about Tamari lattices in a different direction by considering pop-stack operators of ornamentation lattices.
L72: Given a finite lattice $L$ and an element $x\in L$, we let $\text{$\mathchar 525$}_{\mathsf{Pop}}(x)=\{x,\mathsf{Pop}(x),\mathsf{Pop}^{2}(x),\ldots\}$ denote the forward orbit of $x$ under $\mathsf{Pop}$. If $t$ is a sufficiently large integer, then $\mathsf{Pop}^{t}(x)$ is the minimum element $\hat{0}$ of $L$. We are interested in $|\text{$\mathchar 525$}_{\mathsf{Pop}}(x)|$. When considering the pop-stack operator, one of the most well studied quantities associated to $L$ is
L73:  | $$\max_{x\in L}|\text{$\mathchar 525$}_{\mathsf{Pop}}(x)|$$  |
L74: (see, e.g., [cite33†4 , cite35†9 , cite36†10 , cite32†20 ]). For example, Barnard, Defant, and Hanson found that if $L$ is a Cambrian lattice of a finite Coxeter group $W$, then $\max_{x\in L}|\text{$\mathchar 525$}_{\mathsf{Pop}}(x)|$ is equal to the Coxeter number of $W$. In particular, if $L$ is the $n$-th Tamari lattice (which is a Cambrian lattice of the symmetric group $S_{n}$), then this number is $n$; this special case was proved earlier in [cite36†10 ].
L75: Another important aspect of the pop-stack operator is its image, which has been studied for a variety of lattices in [cite33†4 , cite34†6 , cite37†12 , cite38†14 , cite39†19 ]. Defant and Williams found numerous different interpretations of the size of the image of $\mathsf{Pop}$ when $L$ is a semidistributive lattice (or, more generally, a semidistrim lattice).
L76: Notably, when $L$ is semidistributive, the image of $\mathsf{Pop}$ is in bijection with the facets of a simplicial complex called the canonical join complex of $L$ (see [cite40†3 , cite33†4 ]). Hong [cite38†14 ] characterized and enumerated $\mathsf{Pop}$ images on Tamari lattices. Choi and Sun [cite34†6 ] subsequently obtained analogous results for a variety of other lattices.
L77: Barnard, Defant, and Hanson then unified several of these results by providing a simple Coxeter-theoretic description of the image of $\mathsf{Pop}$ on an arbitrary Cambrian lattice of a finite Coxeter group. We aim to generalize Hong’s results concerning Tamari lattices in a different direction by studying $\mathsf{Pop}$ images on ornamentation lattices.
L78: ### 1.3. Main Results
L79: 
L80: Let $\mathsf{T}\in\mathrm{PT}_{n}$. Unless otherwise stated, we will write $\mathsf{Pop}$ for the pop-stack operator on the ornamentation lattice $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$. Define the depth of a node $v\in\mathsf{T}$ to be the quantity $0pt_{\mathsf{T}}(v)=|\nabla_{\mathsf{T}}(v)|-1$. Let $\mathcal{M}_{\mathsf{T}}$ denote the set of maximal chains in $\mathsf{T}$.
L81: ###### Theorem 1.1.
L82: 
L83: Let $\mathsf{T}\in\mathrm{PT}_{n}$, and let $\mathfrak{r}$ be the root of $\mathsf{T}$. Then
L84: 
L85:  | $$\max_{\delta\in\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})}|\text{$\mathchar 525$}_{\mathsf{Pop}}(\delta)|=\max_{C\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathsf{T}}}\min_{v\in C\setminus\{{\mathfrak{r}}\}}(|\Delta_{\mathsf{T}}(v)|+2\,0pt_{\mathsf{T}}(v)-1).$$  |
L86: Let $\mathsf{C}_{n}$ denote the chain with $n$ nodes. The ornamentation lattice $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{C}_{n})$ is the $n$-th Tamari lattice. In this special case, cite41†Theorem 1.1 tells us that the maximum size of a forward orbit of $\mathsf{Pop}$ on the $n$-th Tamari lattice is $n$, which agrees with the aforementioned result from [cite36†10 ].
L87: 
L88: The next theorem characterizes the image of the pop-stack operator on an ornamentation lattice, thereby generalizing a result of Hong from [cite38†14 ].
L89: ###### Theorem 1.2.
L90: 
L91: Let $\mathsf{T}\in\mathrm{PT}_{n}$ and $\delta\in\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$. For each $u\in\mathsf{T}$, let $o_{u}$ be the minimal ornament of $\delta$ that properly contains $\delta(u)$; if no such ornament exists, let $o_{u}=\mathsf{T}$. Then $\delta\in\mathsf{Pop}(\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}))$ if and only if for every $u\in\mathsf{T}$ and every child $u^{\prime}$ of $u$ in $\delta(u)$, we have $\Delta_{\delta(u)}(u^{\prime})\neq\Delta_{o_{u}}(u^{\prime})$.
L92: In cite17†Section 6 , we will prove that every ornamentation lattice $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$ is in fact semdistributive. This means that $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$ has a canonical join complex, the number of facets of which is $|\mathsf{Pop}(\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}))|$. This provides an alternative interpretation of cite42†Theorem 1.2 . See [cite37†12 , Corollary 9.10] for other interpretations of the size of the image of $\mathsf{Pop}$ on a semidistributive lattice.
L93: It is also natural to consider the image of $\mathsf{Pop}^{k}$ when $k\geq 2$. So far, this has not been explored in the literature, largely because it is often difficult to characterize this image. We will prove some necessary conditions for an ornamentation to be in the image of $\mathsf{Pop}^{k}$ (see cite43†Propositions 3.3 and cite44†5.3 ). These conditions are, in general, not sufficient.
L94: However, we will obtain as a consequence a complete characterization of the image of $\mathsf{Pop}^{k}(\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{C}_{n}))$, where $\mathsf{C}_{n}$ is an $n$-element chain poset (see cite45†Theorem 5.4 ). This will allow us to deduce the following explicit generating function for the sizes of the images of $\mathsf{Pop}^{k}$ on Tamari lattices.
L95: ###### Theorem 1.3.
L96: 
L97: For each nonnegative integer $k$, we have
L98: 
L99:  | $$\sum_{n\geq 0}|\mathsf{Pop}^{k}(\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{C}_{n}))|x^{n}=\frac{1-x^{k+1}-\sqrt{(1-x^{k+1})^{2}-4x(1-x)(1-x^{k+1})}}{2x(1-x)}.$$  |
L100: When $k=0$, the generating function in cite46†Theorem 1.3 is that of the Catalan numbers, which we already knew since $\mathsf{Pop}^{0}(\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{C}_{n}))=\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{C}_{n})$ is the $n$-th Tamari lattice. When $k=1$, the generating function is that of the Motzkin numbers; this recovers one of Hong’s main results from [cite38†14 ].
L101: ### 1.4. Outline
L102: cite11†Section 2 discusses basic properties of the pop-stack operator on an ornamentation lattice and introduces some notation and terminology. We prove cite41†Theorem 1.1 in cite12†Section 3 after establishing a necessary condition for an ornamentation to be in the image of $\mathsf{Pop}^{k}$ (cite43†Proposition 3.3 ). We prove cite42†Theorem 1.2 in cite15†Section 4 . In cite16†Section 5 , we prove cite44†Proposition 5.3 , which yields another constraint on the image of $\mathsf{Pop}^{k}$.
L103: We then characterize the image of $\mathsf{Pop}^{k}$ on the $n$-th Tamari lattice in cite45†Theorem 5.4 , and we deduce cite46†Theorem 1.3 . Finally, cite17†Section 6 provides a short proof that ornamentation lattices are semidistributive.
L104: ## 2. Basics
L105: Let $\mathsf{T}\in\mathrm{PT}_{n}$ be a rooted plane tree with root node $\mathfrak{r}$. All of our main results are trivial when $n=1$, so we will tacitly assume that $n\geq 2$. The length of a chain with $\ell$ elements is $\ell-1$. For $v\in\mathsf{T}$, let $0pt_{\mathsf{T}}(v)$ and $0pt_{\mathsf{T}}(v)$ denote the height and depth of $v$ in $\mathsf{T}$.
L106: That is, $0pt_{\mathsf{T}}(v)$ is the maximum length of a chain in $\Delta_{\mathsf{T}}(v)$, and $0pt_{\mathsf{T}}(v)$ is the length of the chain $\nabla_{\mathsf{T}}(v)$. A descendant of $v$ is an element of $\Delta_{\mathsf{T}}(v)\setminus\{v\}$, and a child of $v$ is an element covered by $v$. Let $\mathrm{ch}_{\mathsf{T}}(v)$ be the set of children of $v$. Let $\mathcal{M}_{\mathsf{T}}$ be the set of maximal chains of $\mathsf{T}$.
L107: For $C\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathsf{T}}$ and $v\in C$, let $0pt_{C}(v)$ denote the height of $v$ within $C$; if $v$ is not a leaf, then we let $\mathrm{ch}_{C}(v)$ be the unique child of $v$ in $C$. For a node $v$ with a descendant $u$, let $(u,v)$ denote the set of nodes (excluding $u$ and $v$) in the unique path from $u$ to $v$. We also write $[u,v)=(u,v)\cup\{u\}$, $(u,v]=(u,v)\cup\{v\}$, and $[u,v]=(u,v)\cup\{u,v\}$.
L108: For $C\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathsf{T}}$ and $v\in C$, let $b_{C}(v)=|\Delta_{\mathsf{T}}(v)|-0pt_{C}(v)-1$ be the number of descendants of $v$ that do not lie in $C$. Define $f_{C}\colon C\rightarrow\mathbb{N}_{0}$ recursively as follows:
L109: 
L110: (1)  |  | $$f_{C}(v)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if $v$ is a leaf;}\\
L111: f_{C}(\mathrm{ch}_{C}(v))+1&\text{if }f_{C}(\mathrm{ch}_{C}(v))+1\leq b_{C}(\mathrm{ch}_{C}(v));\\
L112: f_{C}(\mathrm{ch}_{C}(v))&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$  |
L113: In other words, if we walk up the chain $C$, then the value of $f_{C}$ starts at $0$, and each time we move to a parent node $v$, the value increases by $1$ so long as this does not cause $f_{C}(v)$ to exceed $b_{C}(\mathrm{ch}(v))$. Utilizing the identity $0pt(v)=|C|-0pt_{C}(v)-1$, one can show inductively that
L114: (2)  |  | $$f_{C}(v)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if $v$ is a leaf;}\\
L115: \min_{u\in\Delta_{C}(v)\setminus\{v\}}(|\Delta_{\mathsf{T}}(u)|+20pt_{\mathsf{T}}(u))-|C|-0pt_{\mathsf{T}}(v)-1&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$  |
L116: For each $v\in\mathsf{T}$, define $\mathsf{T}^{*}_{v}$ to be the tree obtained from $\mathsf{T}$ by appending a chain with $f_{C}(v)$ nodes to the bottom of each chain $C\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathsf{T}}$ containing $v$. The following definition will give us a strong tool for understanding the maximum size of a forward orbit under $\mathsf{Pop}$.
L117: ###### Definition 2.1.
L118: 
L119: Let $v\in\mathsf{T}$. The $v$-rank of a node $u\in\mathsf{T}$ is
L120: 
L121:  | $$\mathrm{rk}_{v}(u)=\begin{cases}-1&\text{if }u\not\in\Delta_{\mathsf{T}}(v);\\
L122: \infty&\text{if }u=v;\\
L123: 0pt_{\mathsf{T}^{*}_{v}}(u)&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$  |
L124: Figure 2. On the left is a plane tree $\mathsf{T}$. Three of the maximal chains, named $C$, $C^{\prime}$, and $C^{\prime\prime}$, are labeled under their leaves. For each $\widetilde{C}\in\{C,C^{\prime},C^{\prime\prime}\}$, each node $u\in\widetilde{C}$ is labeled with the value of $f_{\widetilde{C}}(u)$. On the right is the tree $\mathsf{T}_{v}^{*}$, where $v$ is as indicated.

L126: See cite47†Figure 2 for an example of the above definitions. For each maximal chain $C\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathsf{T}}$, the values of $f_{C}$ are weakly increasing as we move up $C$. It follows that if $v$ is a child of $v^{\prime}$, then $\mathsf{T}_{v}^{*}$ is a subtree of $\mathsf{T}_{v^{\prime}}^{*}$. This implies that for every $v\in\mathsf{T}$, the tree $\mathsf{T}_{v}^{*}$ is a subtree of $\mathsf{T}_{\mathfrak{r}}^{*}$.
L127: Moreover, the maximum of $\mathrm{rk}_{\mathfrak{r}}(u)$ over all non-root nodes $u$ is attained when $u$ is a child of $\mathfrak{r}$. This implies that
L128: (3)  |  | $$\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}u,v\in\mathsf{T}\\
L129: u\neq v\end{subarray}}\mathrm{rk}_{v}(u)=\max_{u\in\mathrm{ch}_{\mathsf{T}}(\mathfrak{r})}\mathrm{rk}_{\mathfrak{r}}(u).$$  |
L130: We next describe how ornamentations behave under $\mathsf{Pop}$. Consider an ornamentation $\delta\in\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$. We say a node $v$ wraps a node $u$ in $\delta$ if $\delta(u)\subseteq\delta(v)$ and there does not exist a node $w$ such that $\delta(u)\subsetneq\delta(w)\subsetneq\delta(v)$.
L131: When $v$ wraps $u$ in $\delta$, we define the reduction of the ornament $\delta(v)$ by the node $u$ to be the ornament $\delta(v)\setminus\Delta_{\delta(v)}(u)$, and we define $\delta_{u}^{v}\colon\mathsf{T}\to\mathrm{Orn}(\mathsf{T})$ by
L132:  | $$\delta_{u}^{v}(w)=\begin{cases}\delta(v)\setminus\Delta_{\delta(v)}(u)&\text{if }w=v;\\
L133: \delta(w)&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$  |
L134: 
L135: See cite48†Figure 3 .
L136: ###### Lemma 2.2.
L137: 
L138: Let $\delta\in\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$, and suppose $v$ wraps $u$ in $\delta$. The map $\delta_{u}^{v}$ is an ornamentation.
L139: ###### Proof.
L140: Suppose instead that $\delta_{u}^{v}$ is not an ornamentation. Then there must exist $x\in\mathsf{T}$ such that $\delta_{u}^{v}(v)$ and $\delta_{u}^{v}(x)$ are not disjoint or nested. Since $\delta_{u}^{v}(v)\subseteq\delta(v)$ and $\delta_{u}^{v}(x)=\delta(x)$, it must be the case that $x\in\delta(v)$. Then $\delta(x)$ contains nodes in $\delta_{u}^{v}(v)$ and $\Delta_{\delta(v)}(u)$, so it must contain $u$. It follows that $\delta(u)\subseteq\delta(x)\subseteq\delta(v)$.
L141: But $x$ cannot equal $u$ or $v$, so this contradicts the assumption that $v$ wraps $u$ in $\delta$. ∎
L142: Figure 3. On the left is an ornamentation $\delta$. On the right is the ornamentation $\delta_{u}^{v}$ obtained by reducing the ornament hung at $v$ by the node $u$.
L143: Given an ornamentation $\delta$ and a node $v\in\mathsf{T}$, define a minimal reduction of the ornament $\delta(v)$ to be a reduction of $\delta(v)$ that is not contained in any other reduction of $\delta(v)$. Intuitively, a (minimal) reduction of $\delta(v)$ is a (minimal) change we can make to an ornamentation without ruining its status as an ornamentation. Let $M_{\delta}(v)$ be the set of nodes $u\in\delta(v)$ such that $\delta(v)\setminus\Delta_{\delta(v)}(u)$ is a minimal reduction of $\delta(v)$.
L144: We will see that each ornamentation covered by $\delta$ in $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$ differs from $\delta$ only by replacing one ornament with a minimal reduction of that ornament. In the following lemma, we describe which reductions of $\delta$ are minimal.
L145: ###### Lemma 2.3.
L146: 
L147: Let $\delta\in\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$ and $v\in\mathsf{T}$, and let $u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{k}$ be the nodes wrapped by $v$ in $\delta$.
L148: 
L149:   1. (i)
L150: 
L151: We have $\delta(v)=\{v\}\sqcup\delta(u_{1})\sqcup\delta(u_{2})\sqcup\dots\sqcup\delta(u_{k})$.
L152: 
L153:   2. (ii)
L154: 
L155: If $o$ is a reduction of $\delta(v)$, then $o=\{v\}\cup\bigcup_{u\in U}\delta(u)$ for some nonempty $U\subseteq\{u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{k}\}$.
L156: 
L157:   3. (iii)
L158: A reduction $o$ of $\delta(v)$ is minimal if and only if $o=\delta(v)\setminus\delta(u_{i})$ for some $i$.
L159: 
L160: We refer to the ornaments $\delta(u_{i})$ from cite49†Lemma 2.3 as maximal subornaments of $\delta(v)$.
L161: ###### Proof.
L162: 
L163: (i) This simply asserts that each node in $\delta(v)$ is either $v$ or a member of a maximal subornament of $v$. The maximal subornaments are disjoint because if they were nested, the inner ornament would not be wrapped by $v$.
L164: (ii) By definition of a reduction, we can write $o=\delta(v)\setminus\Delta_{\delta(v)}(u_{i})$ for some $i\in[k]$. The tree structure and the connectedness of each of the ornaments ensure that $\Delta_{\delta(v)}(u_{i})$ is the union of the ornament $\delta(u_{i})$ and any other ornaments hanging below it.
L165: (iii) If $o=\delta(v)\setminus\delta(u_{i})$, then $o$ is a minimal reduction of $\delta(v)$ by (i) and (ii). To prove the converse, suppose $o$ is a minimal reduction of $\delta(v)$.
